transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-02
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Arjun (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Daniel, Renee, Omar (joined 16:12), Priya

--- Optional auto summary (auto) ---
Quick recap: run bench, confirm traffic, sizing sim, security follow-ups.

Transcript body:
[00:00:05] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining on time, uh this is Maya from Redwood inference. we do have Arjun and Sofia from the SE team as well. how are you all?
[00:00:14] Daniel: good thanks, excited to dig into the capacity stuff, we've got a spike problem where marketing campaigns create very short sharp bursts and our current hosted provider throttles us.
[00:00:20] Arjun: yeah thanks, do you mind describing the burst shapes? are they sudden delta spikes, or gradual ramps?
[00:00:27] Renee: mostly sudden, like 10-20x baseline for 30-120s, sometimes back-to-back. typical requests are chat completions with long-ish contexts, so p50 token lengths 120-150.
[00:00:37] Maya: okay that maps to the queueing vs prewarmed problem. so today you're hosted with a general cloud endpoint, correct?
[00:00:42] Daniel: correct, LargeCloud endpoints. we've looked at prewarm but it's expensive, and their autoscale takes a minute or so which is too slow for us.
[00:00:50] Arjun: right, two levers here: reserved GPU capacity (committed pools) + burst absorber pools + queueing policy. Redwood usually models request arrival as a compound Poisson with a heavy tail for campaign events, but we'll validate with your traces.
[00:01:06] Renee: compound.. you said compound poisson? that sounds mathy, but ok. can you explain the implications for tuning?
[00:01:12] Arjun: yeah basically burstiness means variance >> mean; autoscalers tuned to mean will underprovision. so you either keep headroom (reserved) or you allow queueing with SLOs. we propose a hybrid: reserved baseline for 95% of 99% of normal load and a burst pool that absorbs short events with a capped token rate and fallback model variants.
[00:01:33] Daniel: model variants meaning smaller quantized models? how much quality loss?
[00:01:36] Arjun: exactly; we can route to a quantized 4-bit variant for non-critical requests and fall back to full fp16 for higher-criticality. for chat it's tricky but you can do prefix detection to avoid quantizing early tokens. quantization tradeoffs: latency + cost improve, but hallucination/quality may shift. we'll tie that to evals in the PoC.
[00:01:54] Priya: quick security question - for reserved GPU and private deployment, what does Redwood require network-wise? we need VPC, SAML SSO, and KMS/HSM.
[00:02:02] Sofia: yes, for Redwood Private we put a control plane and you can run inference in your VPC. We support SAML SSO for console and RBAC. KMS/HSM integration is supported via customer-managed keys; we'll share the integration doc.
[00:02:14] Daniel: perfect. we also need audit logs retention for 1 year.
[00:02:18] Arjun: that's fine, our observability offers token-level traces and per-request metadata, we can configure retention.
[00:02:25] Renee: back to queueing - how do you model p95 latency if you accept some queueing? we need maximum end-to-end 800ms for interactive flows (p95).
[00:02:33] Arjun: so we simulate queueing delay + inference time. inference time depends on batch size, kv cache hit rates, and model flavor. kv cache warmup is actually a big lever: cold KV lookups on first requests add ~50-120ms depending on sequence length and bwd/warmup strategy. if you can prewarm cache for predicted prefixes we reduce exposure.
[00:02:52] Daniel: how do you prewarm at scale? we have many user prefixes.
[00:02:56] Arjun: two approaches: a) proactive warmup with predicted prefixes using recent telemetry; b) reactive fast-warm that reuses KV segments for similar contexts. proactive is better but requires trace or hint from app. our Optimize suggestions will propose a probabilistic prefix set to warm.
[00:03:12] Renee: okay and how does that interact with burst pools?
[00:03:15] Arjun: we maintain warm pools for high-priority routes. burst absorber pools can be ephemeral and may not have warm cache; so you may face a delta latency there. we mitigate with a small prewarmed buffer and by routing lower-critical work to quantized variants that are cheaper to keep warm.
[00:03:31] Maya: wanted to cover reserving strategy: Daniel, you said spikes 10-20x for up to 2 minutes. do you have a baseline RPS?
[00:03:38] Daniel: baseline is 12 RPS across our authenticated chat endpoints. the campaigns push that to 150-220 RPS for short windows.
[00:03:45] Arjun: cool. so naive math: to meet p95 800ms with your model on a single A100-like GPU gives X tokens per second. but better to use a pool sizing sim; we'll run a small sim with your RPS shape, token lengths, and KV hit rate. our typical result is reserved for baseline plus 1-2 GPUs as a thin burst pool to cover frequent spikes, and ephemeral GPUs for extreme events.
[00:04:05] Renee: ephemeral meaning we spin up cloud instances? latency then is terrible, right?
[00:04:09] Arjun: yes, ephemeral has cold start ~45-120s. so ephemeral isn't great for 30s spikes. that's why we recommend a small persistent burst absorber (warm-ish) and a short queue with graceful degradation - e.g., respond with lighter model or partial response when queue grows.
[00:04:24] Daniel: we prefer not to degrade quality often. is there a cost estimate for keeping a 2-GPU warm absorber 24/7?
[00:04:31] Maya: we'll put numbers in the PoC pricing sheet. rough order: dedicated reserved GPUs at commit discount are significantly cheaper than on-demand ephemeral instances for constant baseline + small burst pool. we'll send a table.
[00:04:40] Omar (joined): sorry late, can you recap the proposed fallback policy?
[00:04:44] Arjun: fallback is multi-tier: 1) route to reserved baseline pool; 2) if baseline full, route to burst warm pool (quantized variant allowed); 3) if still full, enqueue for short window (max 6s) with progress tokens or partial response; 4) as last resort, reject with graceful message. We'll parameterize max queue depth per route.
[00:05:02] Omar: and how about billing and observability? we need token-level cost breakdowns and per-route SLO dashboards.
[00:05:07] Sofia: Redwood Console gives per-route latency and per-token cost. We'll expose token breakdowns and can tag requests from your app for internal chargeback.
[00:05:14] Renee: can we test model switching quality - e.g. run same prompts across full and quantized model and see diff metrics?
[00:05:19] Arjun: yes that's part of PoC: we run paired evals on your prompt set. we'll compute BLEU-like preference proxies and hallucination rates and play tradeoffs.
[00:05:26] Daniel: about queueing model, you mentioned compound poisson. do you provide the simulation code? we want to plug in our trace.
[00:05:31] Arjun: yes we'll provide a Jupyter sim. it'll accept traces and model latency distributions to produce p50/p95/p99 and cost curves across sizing choices.
[00:05:40] Renee: nice. what inputs do you need from us for that sim?
[00:05:43] Arjun: 7-day traffic trace with timestamped request arrival, route id, token counts, and a flag for user priority (if you have). anonymized is fine. also an initial KV hit rate estimate; we can infer from warmup patterns.
[00:05:55] Daniel: we can provide that. one more - private on-prem option: we are heavily regulated in EU and might want a private deployment inside our VPC or even on-prem. how different is the capacity planning?
[00:06:04] Arjun: it's similar but you control the hardware pool. you need to size based on your spare GPUs and plan for prewarming. Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem. the main difference is that autoscale latency for cold capacity is tied to your infra; if you have spare idle GPUs you can preassign, if not you'll need to overcommit reserved. Also HSM/KMS integration and air-gapped constraints can add 2-3 weeks to setup.
[00:06:23] Priya: security follow-ups: can you send the SOC2/ISO docs and a brief network architecture for VPC peering?
[00:06:28] Maya: yes we'll send the security pack and a sample VPC diagram.
[00:06:32] Daniel: about quantization: we worry about latency improvements but also tokenization and kvcache compatibility. some quantized kernels handle kv cache differently, causing mismatch.
[00:06:40] Arjun: good point. certain 4-bit kernels maintain identical KV semantics but may have slightly different numerical behavior leading to small perplexity drift. our Optimize tool flags kernels with kv incompatibilities; we'll validate in bench.
[00:06:52] Renee: let's talk numbers — if we keep 2 GPUs reserved (baseline) + 1 warm burst GPU, what's the expected p95 improvement vs no reserve?
[00:07:00] Arjun: depends on KV hit rate. with a 70% KV hit and a warm pool, p95 for your 150 token average could drop from ~1.6s to ~720ms in our sim. we'll run it with your traces to be precise.
[00:07:12] Daniel: that's promising. what about failover across regions? our traffic is NA/EU. we need cross-region fallback.
[00:07:18] Arjun: Redwood supports smart routing by region and can fail over to a secondary region with a model variant to keep latency. we can also do cross-region burst absorb but that adds inter-region latency and costs. we'll recommend region-local reserved pools.
[00:07:30] Maya: quick note on SLOs — when you commit to reserved you get latency SLOs; for burst pools we offer best-effort with alerts and automatic fallback policies.
[00:07:38] Priya: what's the encryption stance for in-flight and at-rest?
[00:07:41] Sofia: TLS in-flight, data at rest encrypted with your KMS; for private we can integrate HSM for key wrapping.
[00:07:48] Daniel: ok let's nail the PoC scope. we want a 2-week bench with three patterns: campaign spike (10-20x short), prolonged ramp (3-5x for 20m), and baseline traffic. objectives: meet p95 <800ms on interactive route 90% of time, keep cost delta <30% vs current run-rate.
[00:08:04] Maya: sounds good, we'll propose that in an SOW. deliverables: a sizing sim, per-route dashboard, quantization eval, and a recommendation table for reserved vs burst sizing.
[00:08:14] Renee: and pricing?
[00:08:15] Maya: we'll share a price sheet with reserved discounts and line items for Private setup.
[00:08:20] Arjun: one more technical caveat — queuing policy tuning: you can allow short queueing for interactive requests but enforce a progressive degradation policy: after X seconds serve partial responses or shorten output. that's usually better than wholesale rejects.
[00:08:34] Daniel: agreed.
[00:08:36] Maya: any blockers or constraints we should know before sending the SOW?
[00:08:40] Daniel: we need the anonymized trace and legal ok for a short PoC with test data. also an internal estimate for budget — we have a weekly cap.
[00:08:48] Priya: legal will require a data handling appendix; please include the data deletion/retention clause.
[00:08:54] Maya: will do. we'll also include the SOC2 docs and network diagram.
[00:08:59] Arjun: final note on KV warmup heuristics: we recommend warming top 500 prefixes per route based on recency-frequency scoring; that typically captures ~60-75% of hits for chat apps and keeps warmup cost reasonable.
[00:09:15] Renee: that heuristic sounds reasonable.
[00:09:18] Maya: alright, quick recap of next steps: Redwood to share PoC SOW, pricing sheet, security pack. NimbusEdge to share 7-day anonymized trace and confirm legal. SE will run the sizing sim and return numbers.
[00:09:31] Daniel: yep we'll upload the trace by Friday.
[00:09:34] Omar: thanks everyone, schedule follow-up next week to review sims.
[00:09:38] Maya: thanks all. we'll target the SOW out by Monday and the sim by the following Wednesday.

[00:09:45] End of recording.

Notes on transcript quality: a few misheard tokens (LargeCloud sometimes transcribed as "LargeCloud" or "Large Cloud"), KV cache shows up as "K V cache" occasionally, and speaker overlaps near join time.
